units.title: Hello, Pascal!
units.summary: Write your first Pascal program and print text and numbers with writeln and write.

lesson.md: A Pascal program starts with the word `program` and a name. The code that runs goes between `begin` and `end.` (with a period). The program runs these lines from top to bottom.

Line by line: `program Hello;` gives the program a name. `{$mode objfpc}{$H+}` is a **compiler directive**: it tells Free Pascal to use its modern mode and long strings. Every program in this course has this line. `begin` and `end.` mark the main block, and `writeln` prints a line.

Text goes in single quotes, like `'Hello'`. Such a text is called a **string**. `writeln` can print several values separated by commas. It prints them one after the other without spaces and then ends the line. `writeln` alone prints an empty line.
`write` prints like `writeln`, but it does not end the line. The next output continues on the same line. A semicolon `;` separates two statements. Before `end` you may leave it out.
Numbers do not need quotes. Without quotes, Pascal calculates: `2 + 3` gives `5`, but `'2 + 3'` is only text. Use `*` to multiply. You can mix text and numbers in one `writeln`.

Pascal does not care about upper and lower case in names: `writeln`, `WriteLn` and `WRITELN` are the same. Text between `{` and `}` or after `//` is a **comment**, and the compiler ignores it. A `{` followed by `$` is a directive, not a comment.
Strings use single quotes, never double quotes. To put an apostrophe inside a string, write it twice: `'It''s late'` prints `It's late`. The last `end` of the program needs a period, not a semicolon.

card: `{$mode objfpc}{$H+}` turns on modern Free Pascal
`writeln('Hi')` prints and ends the line, `write` stays on it
`writeln('Sum: ', 2 + 3)` prints values one after the other
`'It''s'`: write an apostrophe twice inside a string

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Declare variables with var, store values with := and use integer, real, char, string, boolean and const.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value that the program stores. In Pascal you declare every variable before `begin`, in a `var` section: the name, a colon `:` and the **type**. Then `:=` stores a value in it. Read `x := 5` as "x becomes 5".

lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
Next year: 37

lesson.md: `age := age + 1` takes the old value of `age`, adds 1 and stores the result in `age` again. A single `=` does not store anything: it compares two values. You use it in conditions later.

The most common types: `integer` holds whole numbers, `real` holds numbers with decimals, `char` holds one character in single quotes, `string` holds text and `boolean` holds `True` or `False`. You can declare several variables of the same type in one line, separated by commas.

`writeln` shows a `real` in scientific notation with a space in front: `2.5000000000000000E+000` means 2.5 times 10 to the power of 0. The next unit shows how to print it as `2.50`. A `boolean` is printed in capital letters: `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

A **constant** is a value that never changes. You declare it in a `const` section with `=` (not `:=`) and without a type: Pascal sees the type from the value. Constants make code easier to read and to change.
The operator `+` joins two strings into a new, longer string.

Pascal checks types. `count := 2.5` is an error when `count` is an `integer`, because an integer cannot hold decimals. The other way round works: `price := 3` stores `3.0` in a `real`. Always give a variable a value before you read it.

Names start with a letter or `_` and may contain letters, digits and `_`. Upper and lower case do not matter: `Total` and `total` are the same name. That is why a variable must not have the same name as the program.

card: `var x: integer;` declares a variable before `begin`
`const Max = 10;` is a value that never changes

units.title: Operators and formatting
units.summary: Calculate with + - * /, divide whole numbers with div and mod, and format output with :width:decimals.

lesson.md: `+`, `-` and `*` work with integers and reals. The operator `/` always gives a `real`, even for two integers. To divide whole numbers, use `div`: it gives the result without the remainder. `mod` gives the remainder.
`mod` is useful to test numbers: `n mod 2` is `0` for even numbers. `*`, `/`, `div` and `mod` are calculated before `+` and `-`. Use parentheses `(` `)` to change the order.

In `writeln`, `value:width` prints the value right-aligned in `width` characters. For a `real`, `value:width:decimals` also sets the number of decimals. A width of `0` means "as wide as needed", so `x:0:2` prints `x` with two decimals.
`round(x)` rounds a real to the nearest whole number. `trunc(x)` cuts off the decimals. Both give an `integer`.
`inc(n)` adds 1 to the variable `n`, and `dec(n)` subtracts 1. With a second value, `inc(n, 5)` adds 5. They are short forms of `n := n + 1` and `n := n - 1`.
You cannot store the result of `/` in an `integer`, even if the division has no remainder: `n := 10 / 2` is a compile error. Use `n := 10 div 2` instead.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let the program decide with if, then and else, combine conditions with and, or and not, and pick cases with case.

lesson.md: `if condition then statement` runs the statement only when the condition is true. You compare values with `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` (less or equal) and `>=` (greater or equal).
`else` gives a second way: its statement runs when the condition is false. `then` and `else` control only one statement. To run several, put them between `begin` and `end`.
Never put a semicolon directly before `else`. The semicolon ends the whole `if` statement, so the compiler finds an `else` without an `if`. Write `writeln('Adult')` without `;` when `else` follows.
To check more than two cases, write `else if`. Pascal tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is true.

`and` is true when both sides are true. `or` is true when at least one side is true. `not` turns true into false and false into true. In Pascal, `and` and `or` are calculated before comparisons, so put every comparison in parentheses: `(age >= 18) and (age < 65)`.
`case value of` picks one branch by value. A label can be one value, a list like `'B', 'C'` or a range like `'D'..'F'`. The `else` branch runs when no label fits. The whole `case` ends with `end;`.
`case` works with whole numbers and characters, but not with `real` values. It is often easier to read than a long chain of `else if`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for to/downto do, while do and repeat until, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats a statement a fixed number of times. In `for i := 1 to 3 do`, the **counter** `i` takes the values 1, 2 and 3, one after the other. The counter is a normal variable, so you declare it in the `var` section.
`downto` counts down instead of up. To repeat several statements, put them between `begin` and `end`.

lesson.output:
3
2
1
Go!
Added 1, sum = 1
Added 2, sum = 3
Added 3, sum = 6
Added 4, sum = 10

lesson.md: When the start value is already bigger than the end value, a `to` loop does not run at all: `for i := 5 to 1 do` runs zero times. You must not change the counter inside the loop. The compiler does not allow it.
`while condition do` checks the condition before every round. The loop runs as long as the condition is true. If it is false at the start, the loop does not run at all.

`repeat ... until condition` runs its statements first and checks the condition after each round. It stops as soon as the condition is true, so it always runs at least once. Between `repeat` and `until` you need no `begin` and `end`.
`break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.

A `while` or `repeat` loop must change something in its condition. Otherwise it never stops. Remember the difference: `while` goes on while the condition is true, `repeat` stops when the condition is true.

card: `for i := 1 to 5 do ...` counts up, `downto` counts down
`while x > 0 do begin ... end;` checks first
`repeat ... until x > 10;` runs at least once
`break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next round

units.title: Procedures and functions
units.summary: Group code in procedures and functions, pass parameters, return values with Result and change variables with var.

lesson.md: A **procedure** is a named group of statements. You write it before the main `begin` of the program. Then you **call** it by its name, as often as you like.

lesson.output:
Hello!
Nice to see you.
Hello!
Nice to see you.

lesson.md: **Parameters** pass values into a procedure. You list them in parentheses with their types and separate groups with `;`. A procedure can have its own `var` section: these **local** variables exist only inside it.

A **function** calculates a value and gives it back. Its type comes after the parameters, after a colon. Inside, you store the value to give back in `Result`. You use a function call like a value: in `writeln`, in a calculation or in another call.
`Result` works in the `objfpc` mode of this course. Older Pascal code assigns to the function name instead, like `Square := n * n`. Both give the value back.
A normal parameter is a **copy**: when the procedure changes it, the variable of the caller stays the same. Write `var` before a parameter to let the procedure work on the caller's variable itself.
With `var` parameters, a procedure can change several variables. `Swap` exchanges the values of two variables.
A `var` parameter needs a variable: `AddTen(5)` is a compile error, because `5` is not a variable that can change. Declare a procedure or function before the code that calls it.

units.title: Arrays and strings
units.summary: Store many values in arrays, read single characters of a string and use Length, Copy, Pos and UpperCase.

lesson.md: An **array** stores several values of the same type under one name. `array[1..4] of integer` holds four integers with the **indexes** 1 to 4. You read or change one element with its index in square brackets: `scores[2]`.

You can give an array its values in the declaration, in parentheses. `Low(a)` gives the first index, `High(a)` the last index and `Length(a)` the number of elements. With them, a loop always fits the array.
Use only indexes inside the range. For `scores[5]` the compiler warns you, but with a variable index the program may read or change memory that does not belong to the array.
A string is a row of characters. `s[1]` is the first character, because string indexes start at 1. `Length(s)` gives the number of characters, so `s[Length(s)]` is the last one.

`Copy(s, start, count)` gives `count` characters from position `start`. `Pos(part, s)` gives the position of `part` in `s`, or `0` if it is not there. `UpperCase` and `LowerCase` change the case, and `IntToStr` turns a number into a string. These three are in the unit `SysUtils`, which you load with `uses SysUtils;` before the `var` section.
You compare strings with `=` and `<>`. Case matters: `'abc' = 'ABC'` is false. Compare `UpperCase(a) = UpperCase(b)` to ignore case.

card: `a: array[1..5] of integer;` five integers, index 1 to 5
`s[1]` is the first character of a string

units.title: Records, enumerations and sets
units.summary: Group values in records, name your own values with enumerated types and test membership with sets.

lesson.md: A **record** groups several values, called **fields**, under one name. The fields can have different types. You define a new type in a `type` section and end the record with `end;`. A dot gives you one field: `pet.name`.
By convention, type names start with `T`. Assigning one record to another copies all fields, so the two variables stay independent. You can also make an array of records.

An **enumerated type** lists all its possible values by name: `TSize = (Small, Medium, Large)`. `ord` gives the position of a value, starting at 0. `succ` gives the next value and `pred` the previous one. `writeln` prints the name of the value.
Enumerated values work well in `case`. The names make the code easy to read.

A **set** holds values of an enumerated type, characters or small numbers. Each value is in the set or not, and there is no order. You write a set in square brackets, like `[Sat, Sun]` or `['a'..'z']`. `x in s` tests if `x` is in the set. `Include(s, x)` adds a value and `Exclude(s, x)` removes it. `+` joins two sets.
A set of characters makes a long condition short: `c in ['0'..'9']` is clearer than `(c >= '0') and (c <= '9')`. This program counts the vowels in a word.

`x in [1, 3, 5]` tests if a value is in a set
